I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

vignette: Duy sat at his upright piano in a dimly lit rehearsal studio in downtown Chicago, his fingers hovering over the keys but unable to press them. At fifty, the stage had once been his entire world, but after six months of relentless stalking by a former patron, music had become a trigger he couldn’t escape. The man had learned Duy’s routines, watched him pack his violin case, and slipped notes into the wings of the concert halls where Duy performed. When the stalker finally cornered him in a narrow alley behind the theater, the violation was intimate and swift, ending only because a security guard heard Duy’s scream. The intrusion into his creative sanctuary is what makes the present-day avoidance so absolute. He no longer steps into unfamiliar venues, terrified that he cannot assess the danger until it is too late, and he spends every shift at his day job scanning the periphery of his vision, watching other people closely for the telltale signs that someone might harm him. Because he came to believe the institutions that should have protected him had let him down, his mind began to fracture the trauma further, as if his own psyche could no longer hold the event in a coherent narrative. Over the following weeks, the memories did not settle but instead assaulted him in unpredictable waves. There were parts of the event that he simply could not remember no matter how hard he tried, leaving a hollow silence where the confrontation should have been. Instead, sudden pieces would materialize without warning—the smell of wet brick, the sound of a lighter flicking—and then vanish as quickly as they appeared. When a full sensory reliving finally took hold, it felt completely real across all his senses at once, dragging his pulse into his throat and forcing his body into a state of immediate threat. These intrusions didn't just disturb him; they directly amplified his defensive scanning. Conversely, the overwhelming reliving only deepened his conviction that he was a weak person, incapable of shielding himself or stopping the harassment when it mattered. The chaos of his own recollections cemented his helplessness, making the emotional numbness settle in like a heavy fog. As the numbness spread, it made it impossible to feel anything beyond a low-grade hum of dread, which in turn locked him into perpetual vigilance. He had come to believe he was fundamentally defenseless, a conviction that kept him hyper-aware of potential danger in every room. The constant threat monitoring, in turn, blocked the natural processing of the trauma, ensuring that his memory remained fragmented and unpredictable. Every time he refused to walk down a new street or checked his locks repeatedly, he reinforced the idea that the world was inherently unsafe, which only deepened his sense of weakness. The exhausting reality of living in constant defensive alertness convinced him that he was powerless, cementing the belief that no authority would ever intervene on his behalf again. His divorce had been finalized the month the stalking began, leaving him alone in a spacious but echoing condo where every creak sounded like an approach. The numbness and self-doubt made it impossible to reconnect with old colleagues, and the avoidance kept him from stepping into unfamiliar rehearsal halls, slowly turning his career into a distant memory. Now, the nights are the hardest. He finds it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and the quiet of his apartment becomes a canvas for the same old fears. The cycle tightens with every passing week, each symptom feeding the next without respite. He finally walked into the clinic not because he hoped for a cure, but because the numbness had spread to his friendships and his career, and he was most afraid of becoming the ghost of the musician he used to be. He sits across from you now, waiting to see if anyone can finally help him feel safe in his own head.
